results.input: The use of the null integrity protection algorithm EIA0 in the current security context is only allowed for an unauthenticated UE for which establishment of emergency bearer services is allowed.
results.reference: The use of the null integrity protection algorithm EIA0 in the current security context is only allowed for an unauthenticated UE for which establishment of emergency bearer services is allowed.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.4.1, General
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: EIA0 (null NAS integrity protection) is accepted outside the strictly limited case of an unauthenticated UE establishing permitted emergency bearer services. This leaves NAS signalling unauthenticated, allowing an attacker to forge, modify, or replay NAS messages. Rationale: EIA0 provides no integrity verification and is therefore permitted only to support emergency access before UE authentication; all other NAS contexts require integrity protection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 restricts use of EIA0 in the current security context to an unauthenticated UE for which establishment of emergency bearer services is allowed.

results.input: If the AUTHENTICATION REJECT message is received by the UE, the UE shall abort any EMM signalling procedure, stop any retransmission timers that are running, and enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED.
results.reference: If the AUTHENTICATION REJECT message is received by the UE, the UE shall abort any EMM signalling procedure, stop any retransmission timers that are running, and enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.2.3, Authentication not accepted by the network
results.model_answer: An attacker able to spoof or inject an AUTHENTICATION REJECT can force the UE to abort ongoing EMM signalling, stop retransmission timers, and transition to EMM-DEREGISTERED. This creates a denial-of-service condition by disconnecting the UE from EPS services and interrupting registration or other mobility-management procedures.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 behavior: upon receiving AUTHENTICATION REJECT, the UE shall abort any EMM signalling procedure, stop running retransmission timers, and enter EMM-DEREGISTERED.

results.input: NOTE 1: A service request can only be rejected before the network has initiated any procedure which will be interpreted by the UE as successful completion of the service request procedure and which will trigger a transition from state EMM-SERVICE-REQUEST-INITIATED to EMM-REGISTERED.
results.reference: NOTE 1: A service request can only be rejected before the network has initiated any procedure which will be interpreted by the UE as successful completion of the service request procedure and which will trigger a transition from state EMM-SERVICE-REQUEST-INITIATED to EMM-REGISTERED.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.6.1.5, Service request procedure not accepted by the network
results.model_answer: A network must not send a Service Reject after initiating any downlink procedure that the UE treats as successful Service Request completion. Otherwise, the UE may already transition from EMM-SERVICE-REQUEST-INITIATED to EMM-REGISTERED while receiving a rejection, creating inconsistent UE/network EMM state and potentially enabling denial of service or signaling-state confusion.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 NOTE 1 states that a Service Request may only be rejected before the network initiates a procedure interpreted by the UE as successful completion of the Service Request procedure and triggering the transition from EMM-SERVICE-REQUEST-INITIATED to EMM-REGISTERED.

results.input: Upon successful completion of the security mode control procedure, NAS signalling messages shall be integrity protected.
results.reference: Upon successful completion of the security mode control procedure, NAS signalling messages shall be integrity protected.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.4.1, General
results.model_answer: A vulnerability exists if NAS signalling messages sent after successful Security Mode Control (SMC) completion are accepted without NAS integrity protection. An attacker can forge, modify, replay, or inject NAS messages, potentially causing unauthorized mobility, bearer, detach, or configuration actions. Integrity protection is required to authenticate the message origin and detect tampering after NAS security context establishment.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 requires NAS signalling messages to be integrity protected upon successful completion of the security mode control procedure.

results.input: The UE shall enter state EMM-REGISTERED after successful completion of the attach procedure.
results.reference: The UE shall enter state EMM-REGISTERED after successful completion of the attach procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.4, Attach accepted by the network
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: incorrect EMM state transition after a successful EPS attach. A UE that does not enter EMM-REGISTERED after attach completion may retain an inconsistent registration state, causing subsequent NAS procedures, service requests, detach handling, or mobility management behavior to be processed incorrectly. Rationale: EMM-REGISTERED is the normative post-attach state and represents that the UE is attached and has an active EPS mobility-management registration context.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 specifies that the UE shall enter EMM-REGISTERED after successful completion of the attach procedure.

results.input: The UE shall verify the authentication challenge and respond with an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message.
results.reference: The UE shall verify the authentication challenge and respond with an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.2.3, Authentication response by the UE
results.model_answer: If the UE does not verify the authentication challenge before sending AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE, a rogue base station or attacker can obtain a valid response to an untrusted challenge or impersonate the network. This breaks mutual authentication and may enable tracking, denial of service, or unauthorized access attempts.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 requires the UE to verify the received authentication challenge (including the authentication token) and to send AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE only after successful verification. Failed verification requires AUTHENTICATION FAILURE, preventing acceptance of forged or replayed challenges.

results.input: If the UE has no valid native EPS security context, the UE shall send an ATTACH REQUEST message without integrity protection and encryption.
results.reference: If the UE has no valid native EPS security context, the UE shall send an ATTACH REQUEST message without integrity protection and encryption.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.2.2, Secure exchange of NAS messages
results.model_answer: The initial ATTACH REQUEST is unauthenticated and unencrypted when no native EPS security context exists. This creates a pre-authentication attack surface: a radio attacker may spoof, modify, replay, or suppress the request, causing denial of service or influencing unauthenticated signalling. The rationale is security bootstrapping: the UE has no established NAS keys until authentication and Security Mode Control complete, so integrity and ciphering cannot yet be applied.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 requires a UE without a valid native EPS security context to send ATTACH REQUEST without integrity protection and encryption; NAS protection becomes available only after the network and UE establish NAS security keys.

results.input: The network initiates the identification procedure by sending an IDENTITY REQUEST message to the UE and starting timer T3470; the requested identification parameter is specified in the Identity type IE.

results.model_answer: This enables IMSI-catching/privacy attacks: a rogue or spoofed network can send an unauthenticated NAS IDENTITY REQUEST asking for the IMSI, causing the UE to return an IDENTITY RESPONSE in cleartext when NAS security is not active. T3470 supports retransmission, increasing opportunities to obtain the identity.
results.evidence: The identification procedure is network-initiated. The network selects the requested identity through the Identity type IE, sends IDENTITY REQUEST, and starts T3470. Before NAS security context establishment, the request/response are not protected by NAS integrity or ciphering; requesting IMSI can therefore disclose the UE's permanent subscriber identity.

results.reference: The network shall respond to a SERVICE REQUEST with either SERVICE ACCEPT or SERVICE REJECT.

results.model_answer: A network that does not return either SERVICE ACCEPT or SERVICE REJECT after receiving a SERVICE REQUEST violates the NAS service-request procedure. The UE can remain waiting for a definitive outcome, causing service delay, repeated requests, NAS state desynchronization, and a potential denial-of-service condition.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 requires the network to respond to a SERVICE REQUEST with either SERVICE ACCEPT or SERVICE REJECT, ensuring that the UE receives an explicit success or failure outcome.

results.input: If the UE does not hold a valid GUTI, P-TMSI or RAI, the UE shall include the IMSI in the EPS mobile identity IE.
results.reference: If the UE does not hold a valid GUTI, P-TMSI or RAI, the UE shall include the IMSI in the EPS mobile identity IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.2, Attach procedure initiation
results.model_answer: The requirement can expose the permanent IMSI when no valid temporary identity (GUTI, P-TMSI, or RAI) is available. A rogue or impersonated LTE network can trigger an identity/registration procedure that causes the UE to transmit its IMSI, enabling subscriber identification and location tracking (IMSI-catcher style attacks).

results.input: Until secure exchange of NAS messages has been established, the MME shall process a defined set of NAS signalling messages even if the MAC fails integrity check or cannot be verified because an EPS security context is not available in the network (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST, IDENTITY RESPONSE (IMSI), AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE/FAILURE, SECURITY MODE REJECT, DETACH REQUEST/ACCEPT, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST, SERVICE/EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST, CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST).
results.reference: Until secure exchange of NAS messages has been established, the MME shall process a defined set of NAS signalling messages even if the MAC fails integrity check or cannot be verified because an EPS security context is not available in the network (e.g., ATTACH REQUEST, IDENTITY RESPONSE (IMSI), AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE/FAILURE, SECURITY MODE REJECT, DETACH REQUEST/ACCEPT, TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST, SERVICE/EXTENDED SERVICE REQUEST, CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST).
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.4.3, Integrity checking of NAS signalling messages in the MME
results.model_answer: The vulnerability is a pre-security NAS message acceptance window: the MME processes specified NAS procedures even when NAS integrity verification fails or no EPS security context exists. An attacker can inject or spoof such unauthenticated messages—especially attach, TAU, service, detach, identity, or authentication-related messages—to trigger state changes, paging/service disruption, location-update manipulation, or signalling/resource exhaustion. The rationale is bootstrap necessity: before authentication and NAS security mode completion, the network must accept certain messages to identify the UE, perform AKA, establish an EPS security context, and handle initial access or recovery procedures.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 requires the MME to process a defined exception set of NAS signalling messages until secure NAS exchange is established, despite a failed MAC check or unavailable EPS security context. The exception covers messages needed for registration, identity retrieval, authentication, security-mode negotiation, detach, tracking-area update, and service establishment; consequently, these messages are not protected by verified NAS integrity at that stage.

results.input: The MME shall start timer T3413 when sending the ATTACH ACCEPT message.
results.reference: The MME shall start timer T3413 when sending the ATTACH ACCEPT message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.4, Attach accepted by the network
results.model_answer: If the MME does not start T3413 after sending ATTACH ACCEPT, loss of the ATTACH ACCEPT or ATTACH COMPLETE may leave the attach procedure unresolved. The MME may fail to retransmit ATTACH ACCEPT and to apply the specified retry/cleanup behavior, causing UE service delay, stale NAS/MM contexts, or resource retention. The rationale is to ensure reliable completion of attach over unreliable radio/NAS delivery.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 requires the MME to start T3413 when it sends ATTACH ACCEPT. T3413 governs network-side handling of the pending attach completion and supports retransmission/recovery when the expected ATTACH COMPLETE is not received.

results.input: The purpose of the UE requested bearer resource allocation procedure is for a UE to request allocation of bearer resources for a traffic flow aggregate (requests a specific QoS demand/QCI and may send a GBR requirement); if accepted it results in dedicated bearer context activation or bearer context modification.
results.reference: The purpose of the UE requested bearer resource allocation procedure is for a UE to request allocation of bearer resources for a traffic flow aggregate (requests a specific QoS demand/QCI and may send a GBR requirement); if accepted it results in dedicated bearer context activation or bearer context modification.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.5.3.1, General
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: a compromised or malicious authenticated UE can repeatedly request dedicated bearer allocation/modification with high-QCI or GBR demands, attempting QoS escalation or radio/core-network resource exhaustion. Rationale: the procedure lets the UE express requested traffic-flow QoS, including GBR; therefore the network must treat requests as untrusted and enforce subscription, PCC, APN-AMBR, bearer/QCI authorization, and rate/resource limits before activating or modifying a bearer.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 defines UE-requested bearer resource allocation as an ESM procedure for requesting bearer resources for a traffic-flow aggregate, potentially causing dedicated bearer activation or modification. NAS security protects signalling origin/integrity but does not make the UE's requested QoS entitlement trustworthy.

results.input: The UE shall start timer T3412 upon entering EMM-REGISTERED state.
results.reference: The UE shall start timer T3412 upon entering EMM-REGISTERED state.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.3.5, Handling of the periodic tracking area update timer
results.model_answer: Failure to start T3412 when entering EMM-REGISTERED can prevent periodic Tracking Area Update (TAU) procedures. The UE may retain a stale registered state while the network eventually performs implicit detach, causing reachability loss, service denial, and inconsistent UE/MME mobility-management context.
results.evidence: T3412 is the periodic TAU timer. Starting it upon EMM-REGISTERED entry ensures the UE periodically confirms its presence and refreshes its EMM registration before the network's implicit-detach supervision expires.

results.input: If the UE finds that the SQN is out of range, the UE shall send an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with EMM cause #21 "synch failure" and include an AUTS parameter in the message.
results.reference: If the UE finds that the SQN is out of range, the UE shall send an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with EMM cause #21 "synch failure" and include an AUTS parameter in the message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.2.6, Authentication not accepted by the UE
results.model_answer: A replayed or delayed Authentication Request can cause a UE to detect an out-of-range SQN and return AUTHENTICATION FAILURE with cause #21 ("synch failure") plus AUTS. This creates a distinguishable response that can be used to test whether a specific UE/SIM is present and link its activity. AUTS is intended for legitimate AKA sequence-number resynchronization, but its transmission in response to attacker-triggered stale challenges exposes a replay-detectable oracle.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 specifies that, when SQN is out of range during EPS AKA verification, the UE sends AUTHENTICATION FAILURE, sets EMM cause #21 "synch failure", and includes AUTS. Because AUTS is generated from the UE's authentication state and the received challenge, an attacker replaying a previously observed Authentication Request can induce a response different from a generic authentication failure or silence, enabling presence/linkability testing.

results.input: If the UE receives an ATTACH ACCEPT message, it shall send an ATTACH COMPLETE message to the network.
results.reference: If the UE receives an ATTACH ACCEPT message, it shall send an ATTACH COMPLETE message to the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.4, Attach accepted by the network
results.model_answer: Potential state-machine vulnerability: a UE that sends ATTACH COMPLETE solely because an ATTACH ACCEPT was received could be driven into completing attachment by a forged or replayed acceptance. In compliant LTE NAS operation, this is mitigated because ATTACH ACCEPT is received after NAS security activation and must pass NAS integrity protection, freshness/sequence-number checks, and applicable ciphering processing. The statement alone is therefore not a vulnerability unless an implementation accepts an unauthenticated, invalidly protected, or replayed ATTACH ACCEPT.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 specifies that, upon receiving ATTACH ACCEPT, the UE sends ATTACH COMPLETE. NAS security procedures establish integrity protection before protected mobility-management messages are accepted; NAS MAC and sequence-number validation prevent modification and replay of ATTACH ACCEPT messages.

results.input: The network may initiate a GUTI reallocation procedure during an established EMM context.
results.reference: The network may initiate a GUTI reallocation procedure during an established EMM context.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.1.1, GUTI reallocation procedure
results.model_answer: This is not inherently a vulnerability: network-initiated GUTI reallocation is a normal EMM procedure used to refresh the UE’s temporary identity. The security concern arises if a UE accepts a GUTI REALLOCATION COMMAND without the NAS integrity protection required by the active EMM security context. An attacker could then spoof reallocations, cause UE/MME identity-state desynchronization or denial of service, and potentially influence temporary-identifier linkability.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.301 specifies that the network may initiate GUTI reallocation while an EMM context exists. With an active NAS security context, relevant NAS signalling must be integrity protected (and ciphered when applicable); the UE must reject messages failing NAS security verification.

results.input: TS 24.301 allows the UE to accept certain NAS signalling messages without integrity protection before security can be activated (NOTE: these messages are accepted by the UE without integrity protection in certain situations).
results.reference: TS 24.301 allows the UE to accept certain NAS signalling messages without integrity protection before security can be activated (NOTE: these messages are accepted by the UE without integrity protection in certain situations).
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.4.2, Integrity checking of NAS signalling messages in the UE
results.model_answer: The weakness is a pre-security NAS message acceptance window: before a NAS security context is active, the UE may accept specified NAS signalling messages even when they lack integrity protection. A rogue base station or on-path attacker can therefore forge such messages, potentially causing attach/TAU/service failure, forced deregistration, or other denial-of-service/state-manipulation effects. The rationale is bootstrapping and recovery: the UE cannot verify NAS integrity until authentication and NAS security-mode activation have established keys, while some control/reject messages must still be processable in exceptional or initial-access situations.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 NAS security procedures explicitly note that certain NAS messages are accepted by the UE without integrity protection in certain situations. This creates an unavoidable trust gap before NAS integrity protection is activated; integrity checking prevents modification/forgery only after a valid NAS security context exists.

results.input: The UE shall send the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message always unciphered.
results.reference: The UE shall send the TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST message always unciphered.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 4.4.5, Ciphering of NAS signalling messages
results.model_answer:
The requirement creates a NAS confidentiality/privacy weakness: a TRACKING AREA UPDATE REQUEST is transmitted in cleartext, allowing a passive radio adversary to observe mobility-related identifiers and location-management information carried in the request. This can support UE tracking, correlation of temporary identities, and collection of device/network capability metadata. It does not inherently remove NAS integrity protection when a valid NAS security context exists, but it deliberately forgoes ciphering of the request payload.

Rationale: the serving network must be able to read the initial TAU information before it can reliably retrieve/select the UE security context and process the mobility update. Consequently, TS 24.301 requires this message to be unciphered, trading confidentiality for early mobility-management operability.

results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.1.2.4, Attach accepted by the network

This can cause buffer overflow, excessive allocation, parser desynchronization, or inconsistent capability state. Rationale: ATTACH REQUEST is received before NAS security is established and is attacker-injectable; therefore the MME must retain only the received octets within each standardized maximum IE length, treating excess data as invalid rather than storing it.

results.input: The security mode control procedure is used to establish NAS security between the UE and the network.
results.reference: The security mode control procedure is used to establish NAS security between the UE and the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.1, General
results.model_answer: Potential NAS security-downgrade vulnerability: if a UE accepts a Security Mode Command selecting null or weak NAS algorithms, or fails to verify the replayed UE security capabilities, an active radio attacker could influence algorithm negotiation before NAS protection is established. This could enable NAS message disclosure, modification, or spoofing. TS 24.301 mitigates this by requiring integrity protection of the Security Mode Command and requiring the UE to verify that the command’s replayed security capabilities match those originally sent.
results.evidence: The Security Mode Control procedure establishes the NAS security context, including selected ciphering and integrity algorithms. Because initial UE security-capability signalling occurs before NAS security is active, it is a potential downgrade target. The Security Mode Command binds the selected algorithms to the UE’s capabilities through replayed capability information and integrity protection; failure to enforce these checks creates the vulnerability.

results.input: For emergency bearer services, EIA0 and EEA0 can be selected as NAS security algorithms in a SECURITY MODE COMMAND under the conditions described in NAS security mode control initiation by the network (including KSI value "000").
results.reference: For emergency bearer services, EIA0 and EEA0 can be selected as NAS security algorithms in a SECURITY MODE COMMAND under the conditions described in NAS security mode control initiation by the network (including KSI value "000").
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.4.3.2, NAS security mode control initiation by the network
results.model_answer: The vulnerability is an emergency-service NAS security downgrade: the network may select EIA0 (null integrity) and EEA0 (null ciphering) in a SECURITY MODE COMMAND for emergency bearer services, including cases using KSI value "000". This permits NAS signalling without integrity protection and/or confidentiality, allowing a radio attacker to observe, modify, inject, or replay applicable NAS messages when the exception is accepted. The rationale is availability: emergency connectivity must remain possible even when a normal EPS NAS security context or usable credentials are unavailable. It is therefore an intentional emergency exception, but it weakens protection and must be tightly limited to genuine emergency-service procedures.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 NAS security-mode rules allow EIA0 and EEA0 for emergency bearer services under specified conditions. EIA0 provides no NAS integrity protection; EEA0 provides no NAS ciphering. KSI "000" is part of the specified emergency-mode handling conditions, enabling operation where ordinary security-context assumptions may not hold.

results.input: To initiate the UE requested bearer resource modification procedure, the UE shall send a BEARER RESOURCE MODIFICATION REQUEST message to the MME, start timer T3481 and enter the state PROCEDURE TRANSACTION PENDING.
results.reference: To initiate the UE requested bearer resource modification procedure, the UE shall send a BEARER RESOURCE MODIFICATION REQUEST message to the MME, start timer T3481 and enter the state PROCEDURE TRANSACTION PENDING.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 6.5.4.2, UE requested bearer resource modification procedure initiation
results.model_answer: Potential denial-of-service/state-exhaustion risk: a UE-requested bearer modification places the UE in PROCEDURE TRANSACTION PENDING and starts T3481 while awaiting completion. A malicious or compromised UE can repeatedly initiate modifications, or an attacker can suppress responses, causing retransmissions and prolonged pending state. This can consume UE/MME bearer-control resources and delay normal bearer operations. It is not, by itself, an unauthenticated message-injection flaw: NAS integrity protection and replay protection normally constrain forged requests after NAS security is established.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 requires the UE to send BEARER RESOURCE MODIFICATION REQUEST, start T3481, and enter PROCEDURE TRANSACTION PENDING. The explicit timer-and-pending-state transition creates a stateful transaction that remains active until a response, timer expiry, or procedure abort; therefore excessive initiations or response loss can produce control-plane load and service disruption.

results.input: Upon receiving a DETACH ACCEPT message, the UE shall enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED.
results.reference: Upon receiving a DETACH ACCEPT message, the UE shall enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.301, Clause 5.5.2.2.2, UE initiated detach procedure completion
results.model_answer: A forged or replayed DETACH ACCEPT can force a UE into EMM-DEREGISTERED, causing loss of NAS registration and service (DoS). The risk exists if the UE accepts the message without verifying that it is integrity-protected, fresh, and associated with an active UE-initiated detach procedure. The rationale is that TS 24.301 mandates the EMM-DEREGISTERED state transition upon DETACH ACCEPT, making message authenticity and procedure-state validation security-critical.
results.evidence: TS 24.301 specifies that, upon receiving a DETACH ACCEPT message, the UE enters EMM-DEREGISTERED. This state removes the UE's registered EMM status; therefore an attacker able to inject an accepted DETACH ACCEPT can trigger deregistration and disrupt connectivity.

results.reference: Upon receiving a GUTI REALLOCATION COMMAND, the UE shall store the new GUTI and send a GUTI REALLOCATION COMPLETE message.

The rationale is service availability: 5G permits emergency access even when normal registration is unavailable, but that availability exception must be tightly rate-limited and validated.

results.input: The UE processes NAS STATUS messages to report protocol errors or inconsistencies.
results.reference: The UE processes NAS STATUS messages to report protocol errors or inconsistencies.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.6, 5GMM status procedure
results.model_answer: A rogue or compromised access network can inject, replay, or alter a NAS STATUS message if the UE processes its cause or error indication before validating NAS security and procedure context. This can drive erroneous error recovery, abort an in-progress NAS procedure, or desynchronize UE/AMF state, producing a denial of service. The rationale is that NAS STATUS is an error-reporting control message whose meaning depends on the active NAS procedure and security context; it must not be treated as an authenticated network command when integrity protection, replay protection, or message-to-procedure correlation is absent or invalid.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 defines NAS STATUS as a mechanism for reporting NAS protocol errors or abnormal conditions. NAS message acceptance is gated by NAS security processing where a security context exists, including integrity verification and sequence-number/replay handling. Therefore, an implementation that applies STATUS semantics before these checks, or accepts STATUS outside the relevant procedure state, creates an attacker-controlled protocol-error path.

results.input: The UE shall ignore paging messages that do not match its configured identifiers.

results.input: RRCReject can be sent unprotected (including in SRB0 in RRC_INACTIVE), so a rogue node can reject connection/resume attempts without integrity/ciphering and thereby enforce connection-control abuse and RRC-level denial-of-service.

results.input: After successful completion of the Security Mode procedure, the UE applies integrity protection and ciphering according to the configured AS security algorithms.

Applying integrity protection prevents undetected signalling tampering, while ciphering prevents disclosure of protected RRC content. results.input: During the Security Mode procedure, ciphering is not applied immediately (ciphering is applied after completing the procedure), and if integrity verification fails the UE continues using the prior configuration (neither integrity protection nor ciphering). An active attacker able to block, replay, or inject invalid radio messages can therefore repeatedly prevent successful security-mode completion, causing denial of service and prolonging use of the prior, potentially unprotected, signalling state. The timer is a recovery safeguard rather than an authentication weakness; the exposure arises because radio delivery cannot be guaranteed against jamming.

If no successful resume completion is received before expiry, the UE abandons the resume attempt and performs failure/recovery actions, making the procedure susceptible to availability attacks that prevent message delivery.

This can induce UEs to perform access/resume procedures, causing battery, radio-resource, and availability impact; repeated or targeted induced responses can also support presence/location inference. The rationale is architectural: paging must be receivable by idle/inactive UEs before a UE-specific AS security context is available, and PCCH is a shared broadcast-style channel rather than a UE-dedicated protected bearer. Spoofed paging does not by itself grant authenticated network access, but it can trigger observable UE behavior and denial-of-service effects.
results.evidence: ['3GPP TS 38.331 defines the Paging RRC message for transmission on the Paging Control Channel (PCCH).', 'PCCH paging is a common-channel delivery mechanism intended for UEs in RRC_IDLE and RRC_INACTIVE.', 'AS security activation is performed through SecurityModeCommand/SecurityModeComplete for UE-specific signaling and bearers.', 'A UE-specific integrity/ciphering context cannot protect initial paging for idle/inactive UEs that have no active dedicated signaling bearer.', 'Consequently, activation of AS security for a connected UE does not convert PCCH into an integrity-protected or ciphered per-UE channel.']

results.input: An RRCRelease carrying waitTime can force the UE into RRC_IDLE with a backoff timer. Since RRCRelease may be sent unprotected prior to AS security activation, an attacker can spoof RRCRelease+waitTime to repeatedly push UEs into idle/backoff, causing denial-of-service and energy drain.
results.reference: An RRCRelease carrying waitTime can force the UE into RRC_IDLE with a backoff timer. Since RRCRelease may be sent unprotected prior to AS security activation, an attacker can spoof RRCRelease+waitTime to repeatedly push UEs into idle/backoff, causing denial-of-service and energy drain.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.3.11 (UE behavior on RRCRelease with waitTime) and Annex B.1 (RRCRelease: P=+; unprotected prior to AS security).
results.model_answer: The vulnerability is unauthenticated release-induced access throttling. Before AS security/integrity is activated, a UE may accept an unprotected RRCRelease. A forged RRCRelease containing waitTime causes the UE to enter RRC_IDLE and start the associated backoff timer, delaying further connection establishment. An attacker can repeat this after each reconnection attempt, producing denial of service and additional battery consumption from repeated release, idle, and reconnect cycles. The rationale is that, without AS integrity protection, the UE cannot authenticate the sender or detect modification of the release message.
results.evidence: ['RRCRelease contains an optional waitTime information element.', 'Receipt of RRCRelease with waitTime leads the UE to enter RRC_IDLE and apply the release wait/backoff behavior, including T302 handling.', 'AS integrity protection is only available after AS security activation; earlier RRC signaling may therefore lack integrity protection.', 'Repeated spoofed releases can suppress normal access attempts and induce repeated radio-state transitions.']

results.input: The UE shall discard stored measurement configurations when entering RRC_IDLE.
results.reference: The UE shall discard stored measurement configurations when entering RRC_IDLE.
results.model_answer: If a UE retains measurement configurations after entering RRC_IDLE, stale network-provided measurement rules may survive beyond the RRC connection for which they were authorized. On a later connection/resume, those rules could cause unintended measurements, reporting, cell/frequency prioritization, or exposure of radio-environment information. Discarding them enforces RRC connection-context isolation and prevents old or attacker-influenced configuration from being reused.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 38.331 specifies that, upon entering RRC_IDLE, the UE shall discard stored measurement configurations. This makes measurement configuration state valid only within its associated RRC connected context.

results.input: If system information becomes invalid, the UE shall trigger acquisition of updated system information.
results.reference: If system information becomes invalid, the UE shall trigger acquisition of updated system information.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.2.2
results.model_answer: The requirement can be abused for denial-of-service: if an attacker repeatedly causes the UE to regard stored system information as invalid (for example through spoofed or manipulated SI-change/validity indications), the UE must reacquire system information. Repeated acquisition increases radio activity, power consumption, and control-plane processing, and may delay normal access or service recovery. The rationale is that the behavior is mandatory to prevent the UE from operating with stale cell configuration, but it creates an attacker-influenceable recovery loop if invalidation can be triggered persistently.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 requires the UE to trigger acquisition of updated system information when system information becomes invalid. This ensures configuration freshness, but repeated invalidation forces repeated SI acquisition attempts.

results.input: The UE shall use the most recently received system information that is valid.
results.reference: The UE shall use the most recently received system information that is valid.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.2.2
results.model_answer: The requirement permits a UE to replace previously trusted system information with any later-received system information that is syntactically valid. Because broadcast system information is generally unauthenticated before security activation, a rogue or spoofing cell can transmit newer-looking valid SI to override legitimate parameters, potentially causing cell reselection manipulation, access failure, denial of service, or redirection toward attacker-controlled resources.
results.evidence: The rationale is that SI handling prioritizes reception recency and validity, rather than cryptographic origin authentication or freshness protection. Thus, an attacker able to broadcast decodable SI with suitable cell identity and scheduling context may influence the UE's active configuration.

results.input: The UE shall process only RRC messages applicable to its current RRC state.
results.reference: The UE shall process only RRC messages applicable to its current RRC state.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 4.2
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: improper RRC state validation. A UE that accepts or acts on an RRC message not applicable to its current RRC state may undergo unintended configuration, state transitions, resource actions, or procedure execution. Rationale: 5G RRC message semantics are state-dependent; enforcing state applicability prevents malformed, replayed, or maliciously injected messages from confusing the UE state machine.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 defines RRC procedures and message handling according to the UE's RRC state. State-specific applicability checks ensure that messages intended for RRC_IDLE, RRC_INACTIVE, or RRC_CONNECTED are not processed outside their valid context.

results.input: The UE shall not perform RRC resume if resume is not supported by the network.
results.reference: The UE shall not perform RRC resume if resume is not supported by the network.
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: a UE that initiates RRC resume toward a network that does not support RRC resume violates the RRC procedure prerequisites. This can cause the RRCResumeRequest to be unsupported or ignored, leaving the UE unable to promptly re-establish service and potentially creating repeated access failures. Rationale: RRC resume is only valid when the network has provided the required suspend/resume context; otherwise the UE must use the normal RRC establishment path.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 defines RRC resume as an RRC_INACTIVE procedure dependent on network-provided suspend/resume configuration and context. A UE must not attempt the procedure when resume support is absent.

results.input: The UE shall release radio resources upon leaving RRC_CONNECTED.
results.reference: The UE shall release radio resources upon leaving RRC_CONNECTED.
results.model_answer: If a UE does not release its radio resources when leaving RRC_CONNECTED, stale bearer, MAC, PHY, or measurement state may remain active. This can cause unintended use of previously assigned resources, interference, resource exhaustion, or exposure of residual security/context information. The requirement ensures that radio-resource state is cleared when the connected RRC context ends.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 RRC state-transition behavior requires the UE to release radio resources when leaving RRC_CONNECTED, including transitions initiated by RRCRelease or related procedures.

results.input: The UE shall only apply radio bearer configurations that are explicitly configured.
results.reference: The UE shall only apply radio bearer configurations that are explicitly configured.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 6.2
results.model_answer: The vulnerability is unauthorized or implicit radio-bearer activation/modification. If a UE applies an SRB or DRB configuration that was not explicitly provided in the applicable RRC configuration, malformed or malicious signalling could cause traffic to use unintended bearer parameters. This can enable denial of service, traffic misrouting, or use of bearer/security settings that were not authorized by the network.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 defines radio-bearer configuration through explicit RRC information elements and add/modify/release lists. Therefore, UE state changes for SRBs and DRBs must be tied to explicitly received and valid configuration entries; absent entries must not be inferred, retained as newly configured, or applied implicitly.

results.input: The UE shall maintain RRC state consistency across mobility events.
results.reference: The UE shall maintain RRC state consistency across mobility events.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.3
results.model_answer: A vulnerability arises if the UE does not preserve or correctly transition its RRC state during mobility events such as handover, re-establishment, or resume. State desynchronization between the UE and network can cause use of stale radio/bearer/security configuration, failed access, dropped sessions, or unintended resource allocation. The rationale is that mobility procedures depend on both sides applying the same RRC configuration and transaction outcome at the correct time.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 mobility-related RRC procedures use RRCReconfiguration, RRCReestablishment, RRCResume, configuration identifiers, and completion messages to synchronize UE and network state. Failure, interruption, or inconsistent processing of these procedures can leave the UE and serving cell with different assumptions about radio resources, bearers, security, or target-cell configuration.

results.input: The UE shall apply security configuration only after successful negotiation.
results.reference: The UE shall apply security configuration only after successful negotiation.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 4.3.2
results.model_answer: The vulnerability is premature application of an RRC security configuration before the security negotiation has completed successfully. A malicious or corrupted control exchange could then cause the UE to install or use an unconfirmed, mismatched, or weaker security context. This can create denial-of-service, security-context desynchronization, and potential downgrade exposure. Requiring successful negotiation ensures that activation is bound to validated algorithm/key selection and completion of the relevant RRC procedure.
results.evidence: The security configuration must be accepted and applied only as part of a successfully completed security procedure; failed, invalid, or incomplete negotiation must not alter the active UE security context.

results.input: The UE shall only apply network-provided configurations that are valid for the current PLMN.
results.reference: The UE shall only apply network-provided configurations that are valid for the current PLMN.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.2.1
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: improper PLMN scoping of network-provided RRC configuration. If a UE applies configuration received under a different PLMN, it may accept unauthorized or stale radio, security, measurement, mobility, or service parameters. This can cause cross-PLMN configuration leakage, incorrect cell/reselection behavior, denial of service, or weakened policy enforcement. Rationale: RRC configuration is operator-specific and is only trustworthy in the context of the currently selected PLMN; the UE must discard or avoid applying configuration whose PLMN applicability does not match the current PLMN.
results.evidence: The requirement establishes a binding validity condition between received network configuration and the UE's current PLMN. A PLMN change invalidates configurations scoped to the previous operator unless the specification explicitly defines them as applicable to the new PLMN. Failure to enforce this condition creates a state-confusion issue: data authenticated or provisioned in one operator context influences behavior in another operator context.

results.input: The UE shall not reuse obsolete AS security contexts.
results.reference: The UE shall not reuse obsolete AS security contexts.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 4.3.2
results.model_answer: Reusing an obsolete Access Stratum (AS) security context can revive old RRC/UP integrity and ciphering keys, algorithms, counters, or key-chaining state. An attacker able to replay, delay, or exploit compromise of the former context may then cause acceptance of stale protected messages or weaken confidentiality and integrity. The requirement enforces key freshness and prevents a UE from reverting to security material that the network has replaced or invalidated.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 AS security procedures require the UE to maintain and update AS security context state during SecurityModeCommand, re-establishment, resume, and key-update-related procedures. Contexts superseded by a new security activation or invalidated by procedure outcome must not be selected again for later RRC or user-plane protection.

results.input: The UE shall ignore messages that are not syntactically valid according to ASN.1.
results.reference: The UE shall ignore messages that are not syntactically valid according to ASN.1.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 4.3.1
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: accepting or processing ASN.1-syntactically invalid RRC messages instead of ignoring them can expose the UE to parser confusion, memory-safety faults, state-machine desynchronization, or denial of service. Rationale: TS 38.331 requires the UE to discard messages that fail ASN.1 syntax validation, ensuring malformed encodings do not reach RRC semantic/state processing.
results.evidence: Normative requirement: “The UE shall ignore messages that are not syntactically valid according to ASN.1.” A compliant implementation must treat ASN.1 decode failure as a discard condition, not attempt recovery or processing of partially decoded fields.

results.input: The UE shall apply DRX configuration only after receiving a valid configuration message.
results.reference: The UE shall apply DRX configuration only after receiving a valid configuration message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.7
results.model_answer: Vulnerability: improper application of DRX parameters from an invalid, malformed, stale, or unauthenticated RRC configuration. If a UE changes DRX behavior before successfully validating and accepting the applicable RRC configuration procedure, an attacker or faulty network signaling could force excessive sleeping or waking, causing missed downlink scheduling, paging/service degradation, battery drain, or denial of service. Rationale: DRX directly controls UE monitoring occasions and must therefore be changed only as part of a successfully decoded and procedurally valid RRC configuration; when AS security is active, integrity protection further authenticates the configuration source.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 defines DRX configuration as RRC-provided cell-group/MAC configuration and requires UE behavior to follow RRC reconfiguration procedures. A UE should apply configuration only after successful message decoding, validation of applicable conditional/procedural requirements, and acceptance of the configuration. RRC integrity protection, when activated, protects RRC signaling against modification and spoofing.

results.input: The UE shall follow the configured priority rules for cell reselection.
results.reference: The UE shall follow the configured priority rules for cell reselection.
results.gold_evidence: TS 38.331, Clause 5.2.4
results.model_answer: The requirement creates a cell-steering risk when reselection priorities are obtained from untrusted broadcast or pre-security RRC information. A rogue or manipulated cell can advertise attractive priorities/thresholds so that a UE legitimately reselects toward an attacker-controlled or unsuitable cell. The UE's compliant behavior is therefore exploitable for denial of service, traffic interception setup, tracking, or forced redirection; the weakness is the trust placed in reselection configuration, not failure to follow the priority rules.
results.evidence: TS 38.331 defines cell-reselection configuration through system-information and RRC information elements, including cellReselectionPriority and reselection thresholds. Broadcast system information is used before AS security is established and is not protected by UE-specific RRC integrity protection. Consequently, a UE that follows configured priority rules can be steered by a cell whose broadcast configuration it accepts.
